fields.Front: List at least six advantages of a DBMS over a flat file system (the exam asks for three).
fields.Back:
1. Reduced data redundancy and inconsistency ('Street' vs 'St')
2. Programs isolated from the data (program-data independence)
3. Persistent storage even if a program crashes mid-write
4. Multiple users share the data at once
5. A more abstract conceptual view through views
6. Security, integrity and backups (you need a user ID)
7. Generalized query tools (SQL)
8. Multiple user interfaces; enforced standards; reduced development time; centrally up-to-date information

fields.Front: Give the two problems in the orders flat-file example and name the DBMS advantage that fixes each.
fields.Back:
1. One address was typed 'Oxford Street West' and the next 'Richmond St' with 'W', so the data became INCONSISTENT and a search for Oxford Street misses half the customers - fixed by reduced redundancy/inconsistency.
2. The price $76 was stored as an integer and later $76.00 as a real, so the reading code must change - program-data dependence - fixed by isolating programs from the data.

fields.Front: Give the instructor's examples of 'multiple user interfaces' and of DBMS security.
fields.Back: Multiple user interfaces: one MySQL database reached online through JavaScript or PHP by one person and through plain Java or Python code by another. Security: not just anyone can use the database - 'we don't allow anyone to use it; they have to have a user ID'.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: the registrar, the library and the parking office each keep their own student flat file. Name three problems this creates.
fields.Back:
1. An address is stored three times and updated in one place but not the others (redundancy and inconsistency).
2. Every program must know the exact layout of the records.
3. Two programs cannot safely write the same file at once, and there is no way to ask a new question without writing a new program.

fields.Front: When is a flat file still the sensible choice?
fields.Back:
For a tiny program that stores a handful of settings. Flat files are free and very easy to maintain; a DBMS is initially complex (model first, then tables) and needs skilled staff.
Textbook (Elmasri §1.8) gives the fuller list of when to use traditional file processing: a simple, well-defined application not expected to change at all; stringent real-time requirements that DBMS overhead would break; embedded systems with limited storage; and no multiple-user access. Its overhead costs are high initial investment in hardware, software and training, the generality a DBMS provides, and the overhead of security, concurrency control, recovery and integrity.

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §1.3): list the four characteristics of the database approach that distinguish it from traditional file processing.
fields.Back:
1. SELF-DESCRIBING NATURE: the DBMS catalog stores a complete description of the structure and constraints - the META-DATA - so one general-purpose DBMS works with any database. In file processing the structure is coded into each program (a struct or class declaration), so the program works with one layout and no other.
2. INSULATION BETWEEN PROGRAMS AND DATA, AND DATA ABSTRACTION: program-data independence (add Birth_date by changing the catalog, not the programs) plus program-operation independence (an operation's interface is separate from its implementation). A DATA MODEL provides the abstraction.
3. SUPPORT OF MULTIPLE VIEWS: a view may be a subset of the database or may contain VIRTUAL DATA derived from it but not stored.
4. SHARING OF DATA AND MULTIUSER TRANSACTION PROCESSING: concurrency control (two agents cannot assign the same airline seat), OLTP applications, and the ISOLATION and ATOMICITY properties of transactions.

fields.Text: The three disadvantages of a DBMS are {{c1::cost}} (though MySQL and PostgreSQL are free now, some DBMSs are very expensive), {{c1::initial complexity}} (you must build a model and then the tables before storing anything) and the need for {{c1::skilled/trained people}} to maintain it.
On persistence the instructor says that with a DBMS, if a program {{c1::crashes in the middle of a write}}, we know our data is going to be {{c1::persistent}} - we are not going to lose anything.

The DBMS advantage that means programs no longer need to know the byte layout of the data is {{c1::isolation of programs from the data (program-data independence)}}; the one that lets you ask a new question without writing a new program is {{c1::generalized query tools (a query language such as SQL)}}.

Textbook (Elmasri §1.6.1): storing each logical data item in exactly one place is {{c1::data normalization}}; deliberately duplicating it to speed up queries is {{c1::denormalization}}, and the DBMS must then enforce {{c1::controlled redundancy}} by checking automatically that the copies still agree.
